name: Merv
info: Merv was an Iranian city of Central Asia on the Silk Road, on the Murghab river near present-day Mary in Turkmenistan, first founded in the 6th century BCE and razed for the last time in 1788 and 1789.

facts.founded: The first city of Merv was founded in the 6th century BCE as part of the Achaemenid expansion under Cyrus the Great; archaeological surveys show village life on the site from the 3rd millennium BCE.
facts.where: In the inland delta of the Murghab river on the southern edge of the Karakum Desert, about 30 km east of the city of Mary in Turkmenistan.
facts.known: The capital of the Achaemenid satrapy of Margiana; the base of the Abbasid Revolution of 746 to 750; the residence of the caliph al-Ma'mun from 813 to 818; the capital of the Great Seljuk Empire; its libraries and scholars; the Mongol capture of 1221; the Tomb of Ahmad Sanjar
facts.today: The site is preserved by the government of Turkmenistan as the State Historical and Cultural Park Ancient Merv, established in 1987, and is listed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site.

t: Merv grew from a prehistoric oasis settlement into a satrapal centre under the Achaemenid Empire, and was then ruled in turn by Hellenistic kings, Parthians, Sasanians, Arabs, Tahirids, Ghaznavids and Seljuqs.

Abu Muslim declared the Abbasid dynasty at Merv in 748, the caliph al-Ma'mun lived there from 813 to 818, and under the Seljuqs the city reached its greatest size and became the capital of the whole empire from 1118.
The Mongols took the city in 1221 with great loss of life, it never regained its former prosperity, and in 1788 and 1789 Shah Murad of Bukhara razed it and deported its people.
dyk: Merv may have been the largest city in the world in the 12th and 13th centuries, with a population of up to 500,000; Tertius Chandler gave it 200,000 by 1150.
ev: The first city of Merv is founded as part of the Achaemenid expansion under Cyrus the Great
The Seleucid ruler Antiochus Soter renames the city Antiochia Margiana and rebuilds it at Gyaur Gala
The Sasanian Ardashir I takes Merv, beginning almost four centuries of Sasanian rule
Ziyad ibn Abi Sufyan sends 50,000 Arab troops to Merv as a garrison
Abu Muslim declares the new Abbasid dynasty at Merv
The Seljuq Turkmens under Tughril take over Merv peacefully
Merv opens its gates to Tolui, son of Genghis Khan, and most of its people are killed
Shah Murad of Bukhara razes the city and deports its population

sections.origins:
Merv lay in the inland delta of the Murghab river, which flows north from the Hindu Kush into the Karakum Desert. Archaeological surveys have found traces of village life on the site as far back as the 3rd millennium BCE and have linked the area culturally with the Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex. The delta, which the Greeks called Margiana, gave the place a water supply in the midst of dry land and a position on the routes from north-west Iran towards Transoxiana, and at the junction of the route from Herat and Balkh with the route from Tus and Nishapur to Bukhara and Samarkand.

In Zoroastrianism Merv, under the name Mouru, was one of sixteen perfect lands created by Ahura Mazda, and the geography of the Zend-Avesta mentions it beside Balkh. Under the name Margu it appears as part of a satrapy in the Behistun inscriptions of Darius the Great, of about 515 BCE. The first city of Merv was founded in the 6th century BCE as part of the Achaemenid expansion under Cyrus the Great, though later strata cover the Achaemenid levels deeply. The oldest part of the city complex, Erk Gala, was a fortress in the Persian style controlling the oasis; it later served as the acropolis of the Hellenistic city and the citadel of the Islamic one.
sections.growth:
After the Seleucid ruler Antiochus Soter, who reigned from 281 to 261 BCE, renamed the city Antiochia Margiana, he rebuilt and expanded it at the site now known as Gyaur Gala. Its walls there, built one on top of another, are the largest pre-Islamic fortifications found in the Garagum, and a continuous series of Sasanian coins minted at Merv documents almost four centuries of direct Sasanian rule. Cotton seeds from levels as far back as the 5th century CE are the first sign that cotton textiles were already important to the Sasanian city.

Merv gained new importance under the Abbasids. Abu Muslim expanded it, and the walled city of Soltangala, built to the west of Gyaur Gala, became the core of medieval Merv, while Gyaur Gala remained a craftsmen's quarter. Throughout the Abbasid era Merv was the capital and most important city of Khurasan. Under the Seljuqs it reached its greatest size. Arab and Persian geographers called it the mother of the world, the chief city of Khurasan and the capital of the eastern Islamic world. According to Tertius Chandler it was the largest city in the world by 1150, with 200,000 people, and by 1210 it may have had as many as 500,000.

Merv was also known for its textiles: the 12th-century geographer al-Idrisi wrote of the silk and of Merv cotton, which he called extremely soft.
sections.rulers:
Merv was the centre of the Achaemenid satrapy of Margiana. After Alexander's death in 323 BCE it became the capital of the province of Margiana under the Seleucid, Greco-Bactrian, Parthian and Sasanian states. Bactria, Parthia and the Kushans took control in succession after the fall of the Seleucid dynasty. The Sasanian Ardashir I took Merv, and Sasanian rule, interrupted briefly by a Hephthalite occupation from the end of the 5th century to 565 CE, lasted until Yazdegerd III was killed near the city in 651 and the Sasanian military governor surrendered to the Arab army.

Representatives of the Rashidun caliph Umar occupied the city, which became the capital of the Umayyad province of Khorasan. From Merv, Qutayba ibn Muslim led the Arab conquest of large parts of Central Asia between 705 and 715. In February 748 Abu Muslim declared the Abbasid dynasty there, and he ruled Merv as a semi-independent prince until his assassination. Between 813 and 818 the caliph al-Ma'mun lived in Merv, which effectively made it the capital of the Muslim world. The Tahirids replaced Arab rule in 821 and ruled until 873, followed by the Saffarids, the Samanids and the Ghaznavids.

In 1037 the Seljuqs under Tughril took the city peacefully. Merv became the eastern capital of the divided Seljuq state and from 1118 the capital of the whole empire under Ahmad Sanjar. Turkmen nomads pillaged it in 1153, and it passed to the Ghurids in 1192 and the Khwarazmians in 1204.
sections.life:
Merv was a city of many faiths. Under the Sasanians, beside the official Zoroastrianism, it held Buddhists, Manichaeans and Christians of the Church of the East. It was a major centre of Buddhist learning, with monasteries and stupas at Gyaur Kala and Baýramaly, and between the 5th and 11th centuries it was the seat of an East Syrian metropolitan province. After the Arab conquest Merv and Khorasan became one of the first parts of the Persian-speaking world to be majority Muslim, and Arab immigration was substantial; the Chinese visitor Du Huan observed that Arabs and Persians lived there in mixed concentrations. A substantial Christian community remained, and in 1009 the Archbishop of Merv wrote to the Patriarch at Baghdad about the fasting of the Keraites. Ali ar-Ridha, the 8th Imam of Twelver Shia Islam, moved to Merv and lived there for several years, and al-Muqanna, the Veiled Prophet, who claimed to be an incarnation of God, began his movement there.

Merv was one of the great cities of Muslim scholarship, with Samarqand and Bukhara. It produced scholars of law, hadith, history and literature, among them many called Marwazi, and the historian Yaqut studied in its libraries. Yaqut al-Hamawi counted as many as ten large libraries, one of them in a major mosque with 12,000 volumes. Omar Khayyam spent several years working at its observatory, and Nizam al-Mulk founded a library and madrasa. The oasis was watered by canals cut from the Murghab. A workshop of the 9th or 10th century excavated in the 1990s produced crucible steel.
sections.crises:
In 1153 Turkmen nomads from beyond the Amu Darya pillaged Merv at the end of Sanjar's rule. The greatest disaster came in 1221, when the city opened its gates to Tolui, son of Genghis Khan. Most of the inhabitants are said to have been killed. The Arab historian Ibn al-Athir, writing from the accounts of refugees from Merv, described the executions and the torture of the wealthy, the burning of the city and the burning of Sanjar's tomb, and put the dead at around 700,000. The Persian historian Juvayni gave more than 1,300,000. Almost the whole population, together with refugees from other parts of the Khwarazmian Empire, was killed. Its walls had held off at least one earlier Mongol offensive before it fell.

Excavations show that the fortifications were rebuilt after their destruction, but the city's prosperity had passed. Merv became part of the Ilkhanate and was looted repeatedly by the Chagatai Khanate. Early in the 14th century it was the seat of a Christian archbishopric under the Kartids, and by 1380 it belonged to the empire of Timur.

The Uzbeks occupied Merv in 1505, and Shah Ismail I expelled them five years later. Abdullah Khan II of Bukhara conquered it in 1593, and Shah Abbas soon took it. In 1785 Shah Murad, the Manghit amir of Bukhara, attacked the city and killed its ruler Bayram 'Ali Khan Qajar. In 1788 and 1789 he razed it to the ground and broke down the dams. About 100,000 people of the city and oasis were deported to the Bukharan oasis and the Samarkand region. By 1888 the city was entirely abandoned.
sections.legacy:
Merv's architecture is said to have inspired the Abbasid re-planning of Baghdad, and the geographers al-Muqaddasi and Ibn Hawqal wrote of its palaces, groves, gardens and streams. The deportees of 1788 and 1789 were the last Persian-speaking Shias of Merv. Their descendants, known as Marvis, live in Samarkand, Bukhara and the area between, and Soviet censuses listed them as Iranians through the 1980s. They have kept their Shia religion and their Mervi identity and are counted apart from the local Tajiks.

The site consists of several walled cities built close together in different periods and then abandoned: Erk Gala, Gyaur Gala, Soltangala and the later Timurid Abdyllahangala. The best preserved building is the 12th-century mausoleum of Sultan Sanjar, the largest of the Seljuq mausolea and the first dated mosque-mausoleum complex. It is square, 27 metres to a side, and its turquoise dome could be seen, it was said, by caravans a day's march away. Among the remains of Abbasid Merv are the köshks, two-storey semi-fortified palaces of a type unique to Central Asia in that period. George Curzon, who visited in 1888, wrote of walls, towers, ramparts and domes stretching to the horizon. Excavations began in 1885, and since 1992 the Ancient Merv Project has worked there, with the Turkmen authorities. The site lies north of the village of Baýramaly, 30 km east of Mary, in a park established in 1987, and UNESCO lists it as a World Heritage Site.

summary: Merv was an Iranian oasis city on the Silk Road, founded in the 6th century BCE, where the Abbasid dynasty was declared in 748 and which became the Seljuq capital. It was largely destroyed by the Mongols in 1221 and razed in 1788 and 1789. Its ruins are in Turkmenistan.
references: Edmund O'Donovan, The Merv Oasis, travels and adventures east of the Caspian during the years 1879-80-81 including five months' residence among the Tekkés of Merv (Smith, Elder & co., 1882)
notes: Only one article was available (wp/merv.txt); no History of Merv article.

START: the article says village life from the 3rd millennium BCE but dates the first city to the 6th century BCE; I used -550 with circa true. Its Erk Gala section says that fortress was built in the 7th century BCE, which conflicts with the 6th-century foundation; I gave the 6th century for the city and left the 7th-century date out.
END: razed 1788 and 1789 (the lead says 1788 to 1789); I used 1789. The article also says the city was entirely abandoned by 1888 and the area around Merv deserted by the 1800s.
Population: Chandler 200,000 by 1150 and 'may have' 500,000 by 1210; the lead says up to 500,000 in the 12th and 13th centuries. I kept the hedges.

Mongol dead: Ibn al-Athir about 700,000, Juvayni more than 1,300,000. The lead says Tolui is reported to have slaughtered 700,000, while Ibn al-Athir has Genghis Khan ordering it; I attributed the figures to the historians and named Tolui only as the one to whom the gates were opened. The article's Ibn al-Athir quotation mentions Genghis Khan present; I did not repeat that. Sarakhs levies and the 'bloodiest' claim left out.

Seljuq capital: the article says eastern capital of the split state near the end of the 11th century and capital of the whole empire from 1118; the lead says capital 11th-12th centuries. I used the History version.

The article gives the Sasanian takeover by Ardashir I (220 to 240 AD) with no year; the event is labelled '3rd century'. The Seleucid renaming under Antiochus Soter (reigned 281 to 261 BCE) is labelled '3rd century BCE'. Hellenistic note 'fall of the Seleucid dynasty (63 BC)' and the Carrhae prisoners of 53 BC left out for space; Alexander's visit is called legendary in the article and omitted.

'Merv's architecture inspired the Abbasid re-planning of Baghdad' is the article's statement, hedged here as 'is said to have'. The article says the Hephthalites interrupted Sasanian rule 'from the end of the 5th century to 565 AD'.
Du Huan: the article says he was captured at Talas and observed Arabs and Persians in mixed concentrations at Merv; I omitted the Talas detail.
The Soltangala wall holding off the Mongols 'for at least one of its offensives' is from the Remains section.

Left out: the Mongol-built Buddhist temple (controversial), the kepderihana, the pottery, modern demographics (Baýramaly 88,486 in 2009), the twin towns list, the Turkoman horse, the 19th-century Khiva, Tekke and Russian history except the abandonment, the Kara-Khitai conflict.
The article gives the Soltangala founding to Abu Muslim and says he 'expanded the city'; I kept both. Merv 'renewed importance in February 748' used for the event.
The Tahirid dates 821 to 873 as given; 'Tahirid governors of Khorasan' in the lead not used.
